opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's because the company changes so fast that whatever made me useful six months ago might actually be holding the company back today.

When we started, it was just a few of us, and I was basically the chief engineer. I was writing code every day, debugging, reviewing every pull request. That was exactly what the company needed. But once you go from five people to twenty, and then to fifty or a hundred, if I'm still the person who has to touch every line of code, I become the bottleneck. The company literally can't move faster than me, and that's a terrible situation.

So every few months I have to ask myself: what does the company need from me *now*? Not what I'm comfortable doing, not what I'm best at historically, but what's the highest-leverage thing. Sometimes it's hiring. Sometimes it's product direction, talking to users, figuring out what to build. Sometimes it's fundraising, or setting up processes and culture so people can make good decisions without me in the room.

And honestly, that's hard, especially for someone with a technical background like mine. Coding gives you very fast feedback. You write something, it works or it doesn't, and you feel productive. Management and strategy are much fuzzier. You might not know for months whether a decision was right. So there's a natural pull to go back to what feels good, and I have to consciously resist that.

The way I think about it is a bit like a startup's product: if your product doesn't iterate, it dies. The founder is kind of the same. If I don't iterate on myself, I'm effectively shipping version 1.0 of a CEO to a company that's already at version 5. The mismatch grows, and eventually it hurts everyone.

So it's not that I want to reinvent myself for fun. It's that the company is growing, the problems are changing, and if I want to stay useful, I have to grow at least as fast as the company does, ideally a little faster.

r001.rationale: The candidate says rapid growth changes what the company needs and that continuing the old hands-on engineering role would make the founder a bottleneck, so earlier ways of working become inadequate.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the company I'm running today is not the company I was running six months ago, and the version of me that was good enough then is usually the bottleneck now.

When I started Taichi, I was basically a researcher who wrote code. My job was to make the compiler work, make the performance good, write the paper. That version of me was useful for maybe the first year. Then we had a team of ten, and suddenly the most important thing was not whether I could write the best kernel, but whether I could explain to ten people why we were building it and keep them aligned. That's a completely different skill. If I kept being the guy who stays up all night optimizing a loop, I would feel productive, but the company would stall, because nobody was doing the thing only the founder can do.

Then at twenty or thirty people it changes again. You're not managing engineers directly anymore, you're managing people who manage engineers, and your mistakes propagate through layers. Then you start thinking about commercialization, customers, revenue, and I had essentially zero background there. Each of these stages asks a different question of you, and the honest answer at the beginning of each stage is usually "I don't know how to do this yet."

So the three-to-six-month thing isn't a rule I set for myself, it's more an observation of how fast the ground moves at a startup. The company doubles or the focus shifts, and the skills that got you here are suddenly the wrong ones. If you don't deliberately shed the old identity, you keep defaulting to what you're comfortable with, which is almost always the thing you were good at two stages ago.

What makes it hard is that it feels like a loss every time. You were the best at something, and now you have to let other people be the best at it and go be a beginner again somewhere else. But I think that's actually the job. The founder is the person who has to be most willing to be bad at things in public, repeatedly, because if you refuse to grow, the company just grows to the size of your current limitations and stops there.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the company changes rapidly as it grows, making the skills and approach that worked at an earlier stage inadequate and a bottleneck at the current stage.

astra-6.text:
Because the company changes, and the way you work has to change with it. When you have a very small team, you can do a lot of things yourself. You write code, talk to users, and make decisions very quickly. But as the team grows, if every decision still has to go through you, you become the bottleneck.

So you have to learn to build a team, delegate, and give people enough context to make good decisions without you. And that can be uncomfortable, because you’re letting go of things you’re good at to do things you haven’t learned yet.

I think that’s what becoming a new version of yourself means. It’s not changing who you are every few months. It’s asking, what does the company need from me now? And being willing to change how you spend your time, even if the old way was working very well.

r001.rationale: The response explains that as the team grows, doing everything yourself and routing every decision through you no longer works because you become a bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the company’s needs change very quickly, and your own growth has to keep up. What made you effective when you were working with three people may not work when you have twenty or fifty people. Early on, you can solve a lot of problems by doing things yourself. But as the company grows, you have to learn how to build a team, give people context, and let them make decisions.

That’s uncomfortable because you’re giving up something you’re already good at to do something you’re probably not very good at yet. But if you keep doing only what you’re comfortable with, you can become the bottleneck. So every three to six months, I think you need to ask yourself: What does the company need from me now? What should I stop doing, and what do I need to learn?

r001.rationale: It explains that methods effective with a three-person company may stop working as it grows to twenty or fifty people.
